audit_metadata.subject: religious-studies-aqa
sources_consulted: Wikipedia (Maimonides, Amidah, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, Babylonian Talmud, Bevis Marks Synagogue)

findings.lesson_title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
findings.category: Talmud citation — Bavli vs universal version
findings.claim_in_lesson: The Talmud teaches that to save a single life is as if one has saved an entire world (Sanhedrin 37a). Key Fact box: 'one who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world' (Talmud, Sanhedrin 37a).
findings.finding: The lesson presents the universal ('any person') version of this teaching but cites Babylonian Talmud (Bavli) Sanhedrin 37a, which in its standard text reads 'from the Jewish people' (מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל) — i.e. it is the Jewish-restricted version. The universal version ('anybody who destroys a single life') is found in the Mishnah as preserved via the Jerusalem Talmud / Yerushalmi tradition (Sanhedrin 4:9), or in some manuscript variants of the Mishnah itself. The Bavli 37a explicitly says 'one soul from the Jewish people' in its canonical Vilna/William Davidson edition text. Using 'Sanhedrin 37a' to source the universal wording is a Bavli/Yerushalmi conflation — the same category of error flagged in the audit brief.
findings.correct_information: The universal formulation ('any person' / 'anybody') appears in the Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 in some manuscript traditions and in the Yerushalmi. The Bavli Sanhedrin 37a standard text restricts it to 'from the Jewish people'. Both are valid teachings in context; the lesson should either (a) cite Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 4:9 for the universal phrasing, or (b) note that the Bavli reads 'from Israel' while many apply the principle universally, reflecting the Mishnah's universal reasoning (all humans descended from one Adam). A GCSE lesson teaching the universal version is theologically defensible but the citation 'Talmud, Sanhedrin 37a' implies the Bavli and that text does not support the universal phrasing without qualification.
findings.recommended_fix: Change citation from 'Talmud, Sanhedrin 37a' to 'Talmud (Sanhedrin 4:5; universal reading)' or add a note: 'The Babylonian Talmud reads "from the Jewish people"; the universal reading is found in the Mishnah and Jerusalem Talmud tradition.' Alternatively, use the phrasing that explicitly reflects the Mishnah universal version and cite Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5.

findings.lesson_title: The Covenant: Abraham, Moses and the Promised Land
findings.claim_in_lesson: Moses is described as 'the only person who spoke with God "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend"' with the citation Deuteronomy 34:10.
findings.finding: Deuteronomy 34:10 reads: 'Never again did there arise in Israel a prophet like Moses—whom GOD singled out, face to face.' It does NOT contain the phrase 'as a man speaks to his friend'. That specific phrasing ('face to face, as one person speaks to another') comes from Exodus 33:11. The lesson conflates two different verses. Deuteronomy 34:10 establishes Moses' unique prophetic status ('face to face') but the intimate 'as a man speaks to his friend' qualifier is Exodus 33:11.
findings.correct_information: The correct citations are: Deuteronomy 34:10 for the uniqueness of Moses as prophet; Exodus 33:11 for the 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend' description. The lesson should either cite Exodus 33:11 for that phrase or remove the 'as a man speaks to his friend' clause from the Deuteronomy 34:10 citation.
findings.recommended_fix: Change the citation to 'Exodus 33:11' for the 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend' quote, and keep Deuteronomy 34:10 only for the 'no prophet arose like Moses in Israel' statement. Or merge: cite both verses separately with their correct content.

findings.claim_in_lesson: The Amidah is 'composed of 19 blessings (18 on weekdays, with an extra blessing added later)'.
findings.finding: This description is inverted and misleading. The weekday Amidah has 19 blessings — not 18. The prayer is historically called 'Shemoneh Esreh' (Eighteen) because the original formulation had 18, and the 19th (the blessing against heretics / informers, Birkat HaMinim) was added during the Tannaitic period at Yavneh, making the standard weekday count 19. The phrase '18 on weekdays, with an extra blessing added later' reverses this: the weekday count IS 19, and it is on Shabbat/Festivals that the count drops to 7 (the middle 13 petitions are replaced by a single blessing for the day's holiness).
findings.correct_information: Weekday Amidah: 19 blessings. Shabbat/Festival Amidah: 7 blessings (3 opening + 1 middle + 3 closing). The name 'Shemoneh Esreh' (Eighteen) is historical, dating to when there were 18 blessings before the addition of Birkat HaMinim.
findings.recommended_fix: Change to: 'composed of 19 blessings on weekdays (reduced to 7 on Shabbat and festivals, when the thirteen middle petitions are replaced by a single blessing for the holiness of the day). Its traditional name Shemoneh Esreh (Eighteen) reflects the original formulation before a 19th blessing was added.'

findings.claim_in_lesson: Facing Jerusalem in prayer 'is based on the prayer of Solomon at the dedication of the First Temple, which describes God as hearing prayers offered in the direction of the Temple (1 Kings 8:38-39)'.
findings.finding: 1 Kings 8:38-39 is not wrong as a citation but it is narrow — these verses discuss individuals spreading their palms toward the Temple during personal affliction. The broader Solomonic dedication prayer establishing prayers toward the Temple direction begins at 1 Kings 8:29-30 and continues through the chapter. Verses 38-39 are within this passage but concern individual supplication rather than the general principle of directional prayer. The more foundational statement is 1 Kings 8:29-30 where Solomon explicitly asks God to 'hear the prayer which Your servant prays toward this place'. This is not an error per se but citing 8:38-39 alone slightly misrepresents the scope.
findings.correct_information: The practice of directional prayer toward Jerusalem is rooted in 1 Kings 8, primarily vv. 29-30 (Solomon's foundational petition) and confirmed by Daniel 6:10 (Daniel praying toward Jerusalem three times daily). 1 Kings 8:38-39 is within the same chapter but covers individual-affliction prayer specifically.
findings.recommended_fix: Change '1 Kings 8:38-39' to '1 Kings 8:29-30' or '1 Kings 8' for the primary reference to Solomon's dedicatory prayer establishing directional worship.

findings.lesson_title: Life After Death and the Messiah
findings.claim_in_lesson: 'In the Talmud, the world to come is described as the place where righteous souls experience closeness to God.'
findings.finding: This is a broadly accurate doctrinal summary but is presented as a specific Talmudic statement without citation. The primary Talmudic locus for olam ha-ba and the nearness of God is Berakhot 17a ('the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Shekhinah'). Without a citation, students cannot verify or cite it for exam purposes. Not an error in itself but a missing source that could be upgraded.
findings.correct_information: Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 17a: 'In the World to Come there is no eating, drinking, washing, anointing or sexual intercourse; but the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Divine Presence (Shekhinah).'
findings.recommended_fix: Consider adding '(Berakhot 17a)' as a parenthetical citation, or reframe as 'the Talmud teaches (Berakhot 17a) that...' — low priority as this is accurate and GCSE does not require precise Talmud tractate citations.

findings.lesson_title: Shabbat, Home Worship and Sacred Texts
findings.claim_in_lesson: The Babylonian Talmud was 'completed around 500 CE'.
findings.finding: 500 CE is the traditional date (death of Ravina II). Modern scholarship places final redaction in the 6th century, with some estimates extending to early 7th century. The traditional 500 CE date is widely used in educational materials and is not wrong as a broad approximation, but it elides the Savoraim redaction layer (post-500 CE) that is part of scholarly consensus.
findings.correct_information: Traditional date: c. 500 CE (death of Ravina II). Modern scholarly consensus: substantially complete by 500-600 CE, with final editing by the Savoraim into the 6th-7th century. 'Around 500 CE' is an acceptable GCSE-level simplification.
findings.recommended_fix: No change needed for GCSE level — 'around 500 CE' is a standard educational simplification. Optionally add 'though final editing continued into the 6th century' if greater accuracy is desired.

findings.lesson_title: Shabbat, Home Worship and Sacred Texts
findings.claim_in_lesson: The Mishnah was 'compiled by Rabbi Judah HaNasi around 200 CE'.
findings.finding: Rabbi Judah HaNasi (Judah ha-Nasi) as compiler is correct. The date of 'around 200 CE' is a common approximation, though some scholars (following Abraham ben David) date it to c. 189 CE, and others place final redaction in the early 3rd century. 200 CE is the standard educational shorthand and is acceptable.
findings.correct_information: Judah ha-Nasi compiled/redacted the Mishnah in the late 2nd or early 3rd century CE (c. 189-220 CE). '200 CE' is a widely accepted simplification.
findings.recommended_fix: No change needed for GCSE level — 'around 200 CE' is the standard educational date.

findings.lesson_title: Family Life: Birth, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, Marriage and Mourning
findings.claim_in_lesson: Bar Mitzvah at age 13 for boys, and 'in many communities, 12 for girls'.
findings.finding: The lesson correctly states 12 for Orthodox girls. However, it says 'in many communities, 12 for girls' without noting that most Reform and Liberal communities in the UK and US use age 13 for both boys and girls equally. The lesson does go on to explain Reform communities' egalitarian approach in the collapsible section, which partially addresses this, but the opening statement is not quite precise — it implies 12 is the norm across many communities when 13-for-both is the Reform/Liberal standard.
findings.correct_information: Orthodox Judaism: Bar Mitzvah at 13 (boys), Bat Mitzvah at 12 (girls). Reform, Liberal, and Conservative Judaism: both boys and girls at 13 (egalitarian). The opening statement would be more accurate as 'at 13 for boys and, in Orthodox communities, 12 for girls (Reform and Liberal communities typically use 13 for both)'.
findings.recommended_fix: Revise opening to: 'At the age of 13 for boys and, in Orthodox communities, 12 for girls (Reform and Liberal communities typically mark Bat Mitzvah at 13 as well, treating boys and girls equally).'

findings.claim_in_lesson: The separation of milk and meat is derived from 'Do not cook a young goat in its mother's milk' (Exodus 23:19).
findings.finding: The verse is correctly cited. However, the lesson's paraphrase ('Do not cook a young goat in its mother's milk') differs slightly from the JPS translation ('You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk'). This is a translation variation rather than an error — the sense is identical. Both 'cook' and 'boil' render the Hebrew בשל (bashal). The lesson's version matches common English paraphrases used in educational materials.
findings.correct_information: Exodus 23:19 is the correct citation. Both 'cook' and 'boil' are valid translations of the Hebrew בשל. No factual error.
findings.recommended_fix: No change required — translation variation only.

findings.lesson_title: The Nature of God and the Shekhinah
findings.finding: Wikipedia records his birth year as '1135 or 1138', with death confirmed as 1204. The lesson uses 1135 which is one of the accepted birth year variants. This is not an error — 1135 is a standard educational approximation used in most reference works.
findings.correct_information: Maimonides: born c. 1135 or 1138 CE, died 12 December 1204 CE. Using 1135-1204 is standard and acceptable.

findings.lesson_title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
findings.claim_in_lesson: 'Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream' (Amos 5:24).
findings.finding: Amos 5:24 is the correct citation. The JPS TANAKH translation reads 'But let justice well up like water, Righteousness like an unfailing stream.' The lesson's version ('roll down like waters... ever-flowing stream') is the King James-influenced rendering found in MLK's 'I Have a Dream' and widely used in educational contexts. It is a legitimate translation tradition (the Hebrew נִגַּל can be rendered 'roll' or 'well up') but differs from the standard Jewish (JPS) translation. Not wrong for GCSE purposes.
findings.correct_information: Amos 5:24 is correctly cited. Translation variant only — 'roll down like waters' vs JPS 'well up like water'. Both are defensible from the Hebrew. No factual error.
findings.recommended_fix: No change required for GCSE level.

findings.lesson_title: The Nature of God and the Shekhinah
findings.claim_in_lesson: The Shema is quoted as 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One' (Deuteronomy 6:4).
findings.finding: This is the standard traditional translation used in liturgy and education. The JPS 2023 translation renders it 'The ETERNAL is our God, the ETERNAL alone.' The word אֶחָד (echad) can be rendered 'One' or 'alone' — both are academically valid. For GCSE Judaism specifically, the AQA spec and standard educational resources use 'the Lord is One'. No error.
findings.correct_information: Two valid translations: 'the Lord is One' (traditional liturgical, used in prayer and education) or 'the ETERNAL alone' (JPS 2023). The lesson's version is correct for GCSE purposes.

top_3_worst_lessons.lesson_title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Contains the most serious finding (JUD-001): the lesson presents the universal 'saving one life' formulation and cites it to Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 37a, but the Bavli text explicitly says 'from the Jewish people' (restricted version). The universal version belongs to the Yerushalmi / Mishnah manuscript tradition. This is precisely the Bavli/Yerushalmi conflation the audit was designed to catch. Also contains the Amos 5:24 translation note (JUD-011).

top_3_worst_lessons.lesson_title: The Covenant: Abraham, Moses and the Promised Land
top_3_worst_lessons.reason: Contains a verse misattribution (JUD-002): the phrase 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend' is attributed to Deuteronomy 34:10, but Deuteronomy 34:10 only says 'face to face' without the friend qualifier. That specific phrase appears in Exodus 33:11. A student citing this in an exam would cite the wrong verse.

Contains an inverted description of the Amidah's blessing count (JUD-003): the lesson says '19 blessings (18 on weekdays, with an extra blessing added later)' when in fact 19 IS the weekday count. Also contains a narrow 1 Kings citation (JUD-004).
